finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT /me: the whole request body is merged into the authenticated user object and persisted. Any user can set privileged or internal fields on their own record, such as role, isAdmin, id, email or verified status, or a plan or credit balance. This gives privilege escalation or account-integrity bypass, depending on the user schema.
finding.source: req.body: the JSON body of an authenticated PUT /me request, with attacker-chosen keys, e.g. {"role":"admin"}
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) followed by req.store.save(req.user), which persists the modified user and returns it

trace.note: PUT /me handler; the caller only needs to be an authenticated user
Object.assign copies every attacker-supplied key onto req.user with no allowlist
req.store.save persists the tampered user record
The modified user is echoed back, confirming the write

finding.guards_checked: There is no field allowlist or schema validation in this file. No middleware is visible in this directory, since there is no app or auth setup; req.user and req.store are assumed to be set upstream. Even if upstream auth exists, it does not restrict which fields are writable. The sibling route PUT /me/profile (line 11) destructures only displayName and bio, which shows that an allowlist was intended and is missing here. Prototype pollution via __proto__ was ruled out, because Object.assign on a JSON-parsed body sets an own property and does not pollute the prototype. The direct overwrite of arbitrary fields is the defect.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 does Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or validation, users.js:6 persists it, and the sibling route at users.js:11 destructures only displayName and bio, so any authenticated user can write arbitrary fields onto their own record. The user schema and the upstream auth code are not in this directory, so how much this escalates is unknown.

verdict_facts.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or validation, and users.js:6 persists the result. Any authenticated user can reach this and set fields such as role, while the allowlist on the sibling route at users.js:11 is absent here.
